e.etymology: A spelling of Darryl, from the English surname Darrell, brought by Normans who came from Airelle in Calvados, France.
Rose with the -ena ending, a variant of Rosina, the Italian diminutive of Rosa.
A misspelling of Beulah, Hebrew for married, a name the Book of Isaiah gives to the land of Israel.
Linda with the prefix Val-, on the pattern of Belinda and Melinda.
From Italian assunta, taken up, a title of the Virgin Mary that refers to her Assumption into heaven. Italian immigrants brought the name to America around 1900.
From Marie Corelli's 1889 bestselling novel Ardath, titled after a field named in the apocryphal book of 2 Esdras. American girls were given the name in the decades that followed.

A Japanese girls' name ending in ko, child. The first part depends on the kanji chosen; good, fragrant and righteous are common readings. In US records it reflects Japanese American families of the 1910s and 1920s.
A 1980s variant in the family of Sheena, Shena and Shanna.
In Greek myth Cleone was a river nymph, daughter of the river god Asopus, who gave her name to the town of Cleonae. The name is related to Greek kleos, glory.
From the Greek island of Delos, in myth the birthplace of Apollo and Artemis. It was given to American boys in the 19th century, when classical names were in fashion.
A pet form of Blanche, from French blanche, white or fair, a name carried to England by the Normans.
Clipped from Oklahoma, a name coined from the Choctaw words okla, people, and humma, red. Lahoma is also a small town in Oklahoma.
A short form of Lemuel, a Hebrew name meaning devoted to God or belonging to God, borne by a king in the Book of Proverbs.
A spelling of Shirley, an English place name and surname from Old English scir, bright, and leah, clearing. It became a girls' name after Charlotte Bronte's 1849 novel Shirley.
An elaborated form of Verna, a name that arose as a feminine form of Vernon and is sometimes linked with Latin vernus, of spring.
A shortened spelling of Henrietta, the English form of French Henriette, the feminine of Henri. The root is Germanic Heimirich, from heim, home, and ric, ruler.
An English surname with two sources: the place name Barnet, land cleared by burning, and a medieval form of Bernard. Jewish families in England and America also adopted it.

e.note: Identical to the word ether, the old surgical anesthetic.

assoc.t: ether, an early surgical anesthetic; also the crypto coin

e.etymology: A short form of Araminta, a name that first appears in English stage comedies of the 1690s and may blend Arabella with Aminta.
An old American short form of Elijah, said like the second syllable of oblige. Elijah is Hebrew Eliyahu, my God is Yahweh, the name of the Old Testament prophet.
The Portuguese and Italian form of Matilda, from Germanic maht, might, and hild, battle. It was borne by medieval Portuguese princesses and by Princess Mafalda of Savoy.
A mid-century American blend of Jerry and Lynn, built the same way as Marilyn and Carolyn.
An American elaboration of Wanda with an added El-, used in the 1910s and 1920s.
A spelling of Polly, a medieval English pet form of Mary that came by way of Molly, with the M changed to P as in Meg and Peg.
A surname used as a given name, familiar in Appalachia from Estill County, Kentucky, which was named for the frontier militia captain James Estill.
A 1950s respelling of Deborah, Hebrew for bee. In the Book of Judges Deborah is a prophetess and judge who leads Israel to victory.

The military rank used as a given name, a 19th-century American habit that also produced Major, General and Judge. The word came through French from Italian colonnello, the leader of a column of soldiers.

assoc.t: Colonel Sanders, founder and face of KFC

e.note: Reads as a military rank, so people may take it for a title instead of a name.

e.etymology: An elaboration of Verna or Vernon with the -elle ending.
